messages.subject: log-axis not possible anymore (?)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

under R 2.14, I used ggplot2 to create a plot matrix. I used
scale_x_continuous(trans="log10")  to get the axis in log-scale. Now
(four months later; unter R 2.15.0), I ran the same code again and
realized that the axis scale is not correct anymore (the labels are
overplotted as well, one even shows the wrong number but I guess
that's due to some clipping). I then installed ggplot2 with devtools
(see https://gist.github.com/1150934) because I remember that this
once (under R 2.14) solved some of my problems (thanks to Kohske for
the advice). I was hoping this would solve the problem again under
2.15, but it didn't. I am wondering why my former code is not working
anymore.

I checked one of my former minimal examples I posted (see
https://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2/browse_thread/thread/74ded9936428b17e
but also below), and when I ran it, it reproduced the problem. How can
I get the x-axis in log-scale?

In case this minimal example does not reproduce non-log-x-scale for
you, please let me know. I can provide a screen shot.

Cheers,

Marius

Note that I'm working on Mac OS X 10.7.3.

require(ggplot2)
require(reshape2)
require(plyr)

## parameters of some model
p1 <- c(20, 50, 100, 200)
p2 <- c(5, 10, 20, 50, 100)
p3 <- c("group.1","group.2","group.3","group.4","group.5")
p4 <- c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8)
## replications
N <- 1000
## lengths
l1 <- length(p1)
l2 <- length(p2)
l3 <- length(p3)
l4 <- length(p4)
## build result array containing the measurements
arr <- array(rep(NA, l1*l2*l3*l4*N), dim=c(l1, l2, l3, l4, N),
             dimnames=list(
             p1=p1,
             p2=p2,
             p3=p3,
             p4=p4,
             N=1:N))
## fill the result array (dummy here) with values
for(i in 1:l1){
    for(j in 1:l2){
        for(k in 1:l3){
            for(l in 1:l4){
                arr[i,j,k,l,] <- i+j+k+l+runif(N)
            }
        }
    }
}

## create molten data
mdf <- melt(arr, formula = . ~ + p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 + N) # create
molten data frame
mdf <- mutate(mdf, p12=p1*p2) # add p1*p2

## build means (dummy function here)
mdf.mean <- dcast(mdf, p1 + p2 + p12 + p3 + p4 ~ "Value",
                  fun.aggregate=mean, value_var="value")
str(mdf.mean)

## plot
p <- ggplot(mdf.mean, aes(x=p12, y=Value, colour=p1)) +
    geom_line(aes(group=p1)) + geom_point() +
    facet_grid(p3 ~ p4, scales = "free_y") +
    scale_x_continuous(trans="log10")
p

And I will keep track of ggplots further development.

Thank you.

Am Donnerstag, 19. April 2012 16:22:22 UTC+2 schrieb Christoph Molnar:
> Hello,
>
> how can a new aesthetic be added to ggplot2? Aesthetics defined in aes() are passed to the draw-function of the geoms, without modifying anything.
> So this works as I want it to:
>
> df <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = 1:10, tooltip = letters[1:10])
> ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x = x, y = y, tooltip = tooltip), data =df)
>
> But in the next call tooltip will not be passed to the draw function of geom_point.
>
> ggplot() + geom_point(aes(x = x, y = y), data = df, tooltip = "I am a tooltip")
>
> What is the correct way of adding new aesthetics to ggplot2?
>
> If you are interested why I would do something like that: The purpose of this is to write some new geoms, which garnishs the drawn grobs with tooltips for example.
> The gTree of the ggplot2 plot will then be converted to a SVG file using the gridSVG package. The variable which was mapped to
> tooltip before will now be interactively displayed as a tool tip when moving the mouse over this element.
>
> I hope someone can point me in the right direction!
>
> Best,
> Christoph

messages.subject_clean: Avoiding dotplots squished to bottom of plot
messages.body_plain:
As Ben noted, one way is to use 'dotsize', which changes the diameter of the dots... You can also use 'stackratio', which changes the vertical spacing between the dots:

d<-data.frame(ppt=rep(c('a','b'),each=6),
  val=c(1,1,1,1,1,1,1,1,2,2,3,3))

ggplot(d, aes(x=val)) +
  geom_dotplot(stackratio=2) +
  facet_wrap(~ppt)

Unfortunately, for geom_dotplot, the numbers on the y axis are pretty much meaningless and I don't think it's possible to change this. If you want the dots to line up with actual count values, you have to tweak the y range by hand.

-Winston

messages.subject: Re: Error when using facet_wrap on geom_histogram
messages.subject_clean: Error when using facet_wrap on geom_histogram
messages.body_plain:
I'm still not sure that the "correct" behavior should be for the bars in each facet to add up to 100. In the current version, the behavior of facets is the same as the behavior of using an aesthetic like 'fill': the sum of all the bars is 100. I can see why it would also make sense for each facet to add to 100, though; it would be like treating each facet as its own graph.

Anyway, I tried a few different things but I couldn't come up with a simple way to make it work the you want. Maybe the best thing to do is bin and scale the data yourself. It can be done by using ddply() and hist():

library(plyr)
set.seed(204)
dat <- data.frame(val = rnorm(30), g = sample(letters[1:3], 30, replace=T))

# This generates a data frame of counts for a histogram
myhist <- function(df, colname, breaks) {
  h <- hist(df[[colname]], breaks = breaks, plot = F)
  xmin <- h$breaks[-length(h$breaks)]  # Min value for each bin
  xmax <- h$breaks[-1]                 # Max value for each bin
  data.frame(xmin, xmax, count = h$counts, total = sum(h$counts))
}

# Demostration of myhist: this returns a data frame of the counts for
# the whole data frame
myhist(dat, "val", seq(min(dat$val), max(dat$val), length.out=5))
#       xmin       xmax count total
# -3.3133854 -1.9180915     2    30
# -1.9180915 -0.5227977     9    30
# -0.5227977  0.8724962    17    30
#  0.8724962  2.2677900     2    30

# Now do the same thing, but split by group
hdat <- ddply(dat, .(g), myhist, "val", breaks = seq(min(dat$val), max(dat$val),
          length.out=5))
# g       xmin       xmax count total
# a -3.3133854 -1.9180915     1     6
# a -1.9180915 -0.5227977     1     6
# a -0.5227977  0.8724962     3     6
# a  0.8724962  2.2677900     1     6
# b -3.3133854 -1.9180915     0    10
# b -1.9180915 -0.5227977     4    10
# b -0.5227977  0.8724962     6    10
# b  0.8724962  2.2677900     0    10
# c -3.3133854 -1.9180915     1    14
# c -1.9180915 -0.5227977     4    14
# c -0.5227977  0.8724962     8    14
# c  0.8724962  2.2677900     1    14

hdat$countscaled <- hdat$count / hdat$total
# g       xmin       xmax count total countscaled
# a -3.3133854 -1.9180915     1     6  0.16666667
# a -1.9180915 -0.5227977     1     6  0.16666667
# a -0.5227977  0.8724962     3     6  0.50000000
# a  0.8724962  2.2677900     1     6  0.16666667
# b -3.3133854 -1.9180915     0    10  0.00000000
# b -1.9180915 -0.5227977     4    10  0.40000000
# b -0.5227977  0.8724962     6    10  0.60000000
# b  0.8724962  2.2677900     0    10  0.00000000
# c -3.3133854 -1.9180915     1    14  0.07142857
# c -1.9180915 -0.5227977     4    14  0.28571429
# c -0.5227977  0.8724962     8    14  0.57142857
# c  0.8724962  2.2677900     1    14  0.07142857

ggplot(hdat) +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin=xmin, xmax=xmax, ymin=0, ymax=countscaled * 100),
    colour="black", fill="white") +
  facet_grid(g ~ .)

-Winston

Example code:

library(ggplot2);

           127.6596, 136.3636, 127.6596, 130.4348, 122.449, 127.6596, 136.3636,
           142.8571, 136.3636, 136.3636, 136.3636, 127.6596);
time <- rep("10mins",48);
df<-data.frame(time, result);

ggplot(df,aes(x=result)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=10);

ggplot(df,aes(x=result)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=10) +
  facet_grid(~time);

ggplot(unique(df),aes(x=result)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth=10);

The plot is in fact the same as if I plot only the unique values, as in the third plot.

Is this the expected output?

Hi:

Here's a simple example:

DF <- data.frame(group = factor(rep(1:3, each = 100)),
                  weight = c(rnorm(100, 40, 5), rnorm(100, 55, 8),
                             rnorm(100, 75, 10)))
library('ggplot2')
ggplot(DF, aes(x = weight)) +
    geom_density(aes(linetype = group)) +
    scale_linetype_manual(breaks = levels(DF$group),
                          values = c('solid', 'dashed', 'longdash'))

HTH,
Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Dear Dennis,

Found out how to increase line size:

DF <- data.frame(group = factor(rep(1:3, each = 100)),
                 weight = c(rnorm(100, 40, 5), rnorm(100, 55, 8),
                            rnorm(100, 75, 10)))
library('ggplot2')
ggplot(DF, aes(x = weight)) +

   geom_density(aes(linetype = group), size=2) +

   scale_linetype_manual(breaks = levels(DF$group),
                         values = c('solid', 'dashed', 'longdash'))

Thanks again, Dennis!

Cheers Trong.

Hi all,

I'm trying to use geom_raster to plot the bathymetry of my area of
interest.
I downloaded an xyz txt file from http://topex.ucsd.edu and uploaded
the data into R as follow:

SF.bath <- read.table("SF_bath.txt",
header=F,col.names=c("long","lat","z"))#

> head(SF.bath)
       lon     lat   z
1 292.0083 50.9968 757
2 292.0250 50.9968 693
3 292.0417 50.9968 673
4 292.0583 50.9968 769
5 292.0750 50.9968 761
6 292.0916 50.9968 733

I can plot my data as a raster image using the following code:

P<- ggplot(SF.bath, aes(lon, lat, fill = z)) +
  geom_tile(colour = "white") + scale_fill_gradient(low="darkblue",
high="black")
P

However, when I use geom_raster I get an error message as follow:
newp<-qplot(lon, lat, data = SF.bath, fill = z, geom = "raster")
> newp
Using alpha as value column: use value_var to override.

I'm not sure what I need to do to fix this.

Thank you very much in advance,
Aurelie

messages.subject: Re: annotate "rect" in new ggplot2
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I just want to reopen an issue we had some weeks ago about extending the plot and drawing rectangles etc. (see correspondence below)
Therefore Takahashi Kohske helped me by using coord_cartesian.
This worked for nearly all of my plots but now I realised that there
is still a little problem with one plot where my x-axis disappeared.
So I tried to find the problem and found it. Here small
example to reproduce it:

y <- runif(1000,0.01,50000)
x <- runif(1000,39,810)
df <- data.frame(x,y)

plot.length <- ggplot(df, aes(x=x,y=y))+
		geom_point()+
		scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(100,200,400,800),trans="log")+
		annotate("rect", xmin=0, xmax=10000, ymin=80000, ymax=50000000, fill="blue")+
		coord_cartesian(xlim = range(df$x), ylim = c(0.01,100000), wise = TRUE)

The problem with the missing x-axis seems to be related to the xlim parameter and the log-scale. Both together don't work in my case. The reason why it worked for my other plots (also with log scale) was related to different xlims. E.g. if I try to set xlim = c(1,810) it works.

Any suggestions how to solve that problem?

Best regards,
Johannes

barplots. Building gradient circles on other gradient circles, not
unlike genome atlases. I would like to base this gradient on the
temperature data that I have, the gradient going from low temperature
indicated by let's say blue to high temperature with red color, and
then have a legend for the temperature, low, medium, high or 5, 10,
15, 20°C.

Is there a way to incorporate all information in one graph?

I would greatly appreciate any help you can provide.

messages.subject: cleaning up a plot
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to clean up a set of forest plots.

Thus far, thanks to suggestions on this list serve, I have 3 to 4 parameters that I am plotting (pharmacokinetic parameters) for 4 different drugs using a coord_flip + geom_errorbar to display the fold-change in each parameter in different conditions.

iv.mdz2<-ggplot(ivmdz2, aes(x=Parameter, y=Mean, ymin=Lo, ymax=Hi))
iv.mdz2<-iv.mdz2+geom_errorbar()+coord_flip()+geom_hline(aes(yintercept=0), lty=2)+xlab('Parameter') +ylab("Fold Change with 90% CI") + geom_point(aes(x=Parameter, y=Mean), size=8, shape=5)+theme_bw()
iv.mdz2<-iv.mdz2+scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-1,3))+ opts(title="xxx")
iv.mdz2

For publication, I would like to both plot 4 of these plots in a grid, with the parameter name on the x, and the fold change on the y (mock-up below).   To do this, I need to be able to re-order the parameters, and fit this to a facet_grid.   Any help in this would be appreciated.

Thanks

--
R. Matthew Strother, MD
Clinical Pharmacology
Medical Oncology

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Tue, Apr 24, 2012 at 3:38 PM, Rebecca Clark <rebecc...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello, ggplot2 gurus,
>
> I have a dataset consisting of two dependent variables and one independent
> variable, like so:
>

> measures<-data.frame(A=c(28.27, 65.32, 139.00, 179.28, 176.56, 93.25),

                                    B=c(141.38, 130.63, 139.00,
> 89.64, 35.31, 151.41), p=c(7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 16))
>
> abplot<-ggplot(measures, aes(A, B))+geom_point()
>
> In this case, the error variances are approximately equal for both A and B,
> and both are measured in the same unit.  When I've added together A and B
> and regressed them against the third (independent) variable, p, a
> second-order polynomial fit has higher explanatory power than a linear fit.

I had to read this a couple of times before I think I got it: is this
what you're looking for?

ggplot(measures, aes(x = p, y = A + B)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() +
    geom_smooth(method = 'lm', colour = 'red', fill = 'red', alpha = 0.1) +
    geom_smooth(method = 'lm', colour = 'blue', formula = y ~ poly(x, 2),
                  fill = 'blue', alpha = 0.1)

The advantage of adding the confidence bands to the plot is to show
that the quadratic model in p has tighter confidence bands than the
corresponding linear model. Observe that in the second call to
geom_smooth, the formula uses y as the response and x as the single
covariate rather than the actual names of the covariate and response.
poly(x, 2) fits a quadratic polynomial model in x.

>
> My question is this: the default method for geom_smooth() uses ordinary
> least squares regression to minimize variance on y (right?).  Is it somehow
> possible to add the appropriate polynomial curve to this graph - one that
> minimizes variance on both x and y?

Actually, the default method for geom_smooth() is loess, a popular
nonparametric smoother; try

ggplot(measures, aes(x = p, y = A + B)) + geom_point() + theme_bw() +
     geom_smooth()

The resulting warnings indicate that loess seriously overfits these
data, which is evident from the plot generated by the above code.
(This is a consequence of the small sample size - it really makes no
sense to fit a loess model when n is this small.) The first and
second-order linear models in p both use OLS.

I don't know what your last parenthetical comment means - OLS
minimizes the residual sum of squares, but does not minimize variance
in either x or y (except perhaps by coincidence).

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: coord_flip confussion / feature request
messages.body_plain:
I'm wondering what the rationale for having coord_flip() is. In my
view the use of it is mostly related to having box-and-whiskers,
violin, line range etc. plot flipped over.

I would think that the two former should just draw their orientation
from whether x or y are factor values and linerange should have an
x_linerange and y_linerange parallel. In my view this allows for far
more flexibility (especially in facetted plots), but is also more
intuitive...

e.g. given 'data' is our data.frame, class is a factor and value is
numeric:

p <- ggplot(data=data)

p + geom_boxplot(aes(x=factor, y=value))

could be flipped simply by:

p + geom_boxplot(aes(x=value, y=factor))

I don't think that coord_flip should necessary be abandoned but i
believe it is an unnecessary constraint that some geom orientation is
dependent on it...

Does this make sense for others

best wishes

Thomas

messages.body_plain:
I can't answer your question about using TLS, but once you have the TLS model object, it's possible to plot the line without using stat_smooth() -- in fact, it's probably a better idea to not use stat_smooth() in a case like this because it's hard to make sure that it's using the same model that you generate yourself.

Generally speaking, model objects have an associated predict() method. For example, lm objects have predict.lm(); glm objects have predict.glm(), and so on. The specific methods are called automatically when you pass the model object to the non-specific predict() method. Assuming that there's a predict method for tls, you could do something like this, replacing the model with whatever you come up with:

measures <- data.frame(

  A=c(28.27, 65.32, 139.00, 179.28, 176.56, 93.25),
  B=c(141.38, 130.63, 139.00, 89.64, 35.31, 151.41),
  p=c(7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 16))

# Make the model - quadratic lm in this case
model <- lm(B ~ A + I(A^2), data=measures)

# Need to create a new data frame with predictor (A) values spanning the range
# of A from the original data in measures
minA <- min(measures$A)
maxA <- max(measures$A)
newdata <- data.frame(A = seq(minA, maxA, length.out=100))

# Predict values across the range
newdata$B <- predict(model, newdata)

# Plot the original points with a line of predicted values
ggplot(measures, aes(x=A, y=B)) + geom_point() + geom_line(data=newdata)

-Winston

messages.body_plain:
>For publication, I would like to both plot 4 of these plots in a grid, with the parameter name on the x, and the fold change on the y (mock-up below).   To do this, I need to be able to re-order the parameters, and fit this to a facet_grid.   Any help in this would be appreciated.

Robert, here's my first crack at it. See code below.
Regards,
Ben

d <- read.csv("ivmdz2.csv")

library( ggplot2 )
library( grid )

p <- ggplot( d, aes( x=Parameter, y=Mean, ymin=Lo, ymax=Hi ) )

p <- p + geom_errorbar() + coord_flip() + geom_hline( aes( yintercept=0 ), lty=2 )
p <- p + xlab( 'Parameter' ) +ylab( "Fold Change with 90% CI" ) + geom_point( size=3, shape=5 )
p <- p + scale_y_continuous( limits=c( -1, 3 ) ) + opts( title="xxx" )
p <- p + facet_wrap( ~Drug, nrow=2, ncol=2 )
p <- p + theme_bw() + opts( strip.text.x=theme_blank(), strip.background=theme_blank() )

print( p )

grid.text( "A", 0.16, 0.9, gp=gpar( fontface="bold" ) )      # A-D annotations
grid.text( "B", 0.58, 0.9, gp=gpar( fontface="bold" ) )
grid.text( "C", 0.16, 0.47, gp=gpar( fontface="bold" ) )
grid.text( "D", 0.58, 0.47, gp=gpar( fontface="bold" ) )

messages.subject: Re: microbial dynamics
messages.body_plain:
As I said in the initial reply, the architecture right now does not
support multiple fill scales. This means that it is not easy to have
multiple rings in one plot. I have overcome this by building the heat
maps manually using a lot of for loops, but this can get quite
heavy...

The second problem is that I did not realize that the fill scale was
already used for building the stacked bar/pie chart, so even one outer
ring would require some data joggling...

to create your outer rings it will be necessary to manually calculate
the associated color for each tile and build the ring iteratively in a
for loop like:

for (i in 1:nrow(data.a)){
  p <- p + geom_tile(data=data.a[i, 'Salinity'], aes(x=Date, y=y.pos),
fill=colour, width=1, height=tile.height)
}

where y.pos is a value higher than the height of your barplot,
tile.height is the width of the ring and color is your calculated
color for the single tile.

The problem with this approach is that you do not get legends
associated with the rings, but it is the best I can think of...

good luck

Thomas

messages.subject: theme_<journal_name> library
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Working in research, like I'm sure a reasonable number of others do, I
have to produce graphs for journals. When it's for a powerpoint
presentation or email for discussion among colleagues, graphics are
easy, but when you have the journals strict specifications (this may
be my lack of skills) tweaking everything can be a right pain, and
consume hours.

Using my recent experiences as examples, some journals have 2.2 inch
columns (3 col) others 8.6cm columns (2col). Of course producing
graphs for these requires quite different settings, font sizes, point
sizes, line widths, axis tick mark lengths etc.

This may have been floated before, but would others find value in
having an (unofficial) theme database for journals, where users can
contribute the themes they set up?

In the same way endnote has gone from having APA and Harvard styles
(think theme_grey and theme_bw) to having almost all journals custom
bib formats listed, we could have theme_nature theme_stroke
theme_microbiology etc.

I have more thoughts on this but figure that's enough to gauge the
response.

Cheers

messages.subject: Re: coord_flip confussion / feature request
messages.body_plain:
On 4/25/2012 1:45 AM, Thomas wrote:
> I'm wondering what the rationale for having coord_flip() is. In my
> view the use of it is mostly related to having box-and-whiskers,
> violin, line range etc. plot flipped over.
>
> I would think that the two former should just draw their orientation
> from whether x or y are factor values and linerange should have an
> x_linerange and y_linerange parallel. In my view this allows for far
> more flexibility (especially in facetted plots), but is also more
> intuitive...
>
> e.g. given 'data' is our data.frame, class is a factor and value is
> numeric:
>
> p<- ggplot(data=data)
>
> p + geom_boxplot(aes(x=factor, y=value))
>
> could be flipped simply by:
>
> p + geom_boxplot(aes(x=value, y=factor))
>
> I don't think that coord_flip should necessary be abandoned but i
> believe it is an unnecessary constraint that some geom orientation is
> dependent on it...
>
> Does this make sense for others

Eliminating the need for coord_flip() makes sense to me. It is something
I put on the wishlist
(https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/wishlist---feature-requests)
back when a few of us were brainstorming things we'd like to see.

I don't know if I would implement it as determining the direction based
on which dimensions are continuous and which are discrete. While this
would work for boxplot, it would not work for linerange/pointrange (as
you note). It would be problematic for density and histogram as well.

Hadley mentioned once the idea of a function which would take a geom and
return a flipped geom. I think that would be a good approach because
then there would not be effectively duplicated code in a geom that just
acted on different dimensions.  That isn't something I'd want to try
until after the geom re-write from proto to S3.

> best wishes
>
> Thomas
>

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

> having an (unofficial) theme database for journals, where users can
> contribute the themes they set up?
>
> In the same way endnote has gone from having APA and Harvard styles
> (think theme_grey and theme_bw) to having almost all journals custom
> bib formats listed, we could have theme_nature theme_stroke
> theme_microbiology etc.
>
> I have more thoughts on this but figure that's enough to gauge the
> response.
>
> Cheers

A start on this is the theme gallery at
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Themes There are not any journal
specific themes there, but there is no reason there couldn't be.

way to go. That is not something that should be coupled to the ggplot2
release cycle.

messages.body_plain:
Hey there,

I started making related adjustments with theme_minimal from the github page for myself, too.  I had to tweak a couple of lines in theme_minimal to get it to play nicely with version 0.9.0 - for some reason at the time I used it, I think I had to switch the units for axis.ticks.length and axis.ticks.margin from "lines" to "cm".

Other than that, I have generally been saving plots using the journal's requested final dimensions, and you'll note that fonts, font sizes and line sizes should remain appropriate if you do that (because base.size is set at 12 and the default sans serif font is Helvetica).  Using ggplot2 for this has saved me a lot of those painful hours, especially when I have to go back and change something in the original dataset and analysis for some reason (which inevitably happens) - my plots are basically publication-ready by the point where I use ggsave().

Here's my tweaked version of theme_minimal, which might be really close to what you'd want.  Also remember to use theme_get() (no argument) to see the settings of the current plot in the quartz window in case there's a fiddly bit that you want to fiddle with.  I agree with Brian - themes are going to get tweaked more frequently than ggplot2 itself, so the github page seems like a logical place to keep updated and expanded themes.

   theme_minimal <- function (base_size = 12, base_family = "")
     {
         structure(list(axis.line = theme_segment(),
                        axis.text.x = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8, lineheight = 0.9, vjust = 1, colour="black"),
                        axis.text.y = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8, lineheight = 0.9, hjust = 1, colour="black"),
                        axis.ticks = theme_segment(colour = "black"),
                        axis.title.x = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size, vjust = -0.5, hjust=0.5),
                        axis.title.y = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size, angle = 90, vjust = 0.2),
                        axis.ticks.length = unit(0.15, "cm"),
                        axis.ticks.margin = unit(0.1, "cm"),
                        legend.background = theme_rect(colour = NA),
                        legend.key = theme_rect(colour = NA),
                        legend.key.size = unit(1.2, "lines"),
                        legend.key.height = NULL,
                        legend.key.width = NULL,
                        legend.text = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8),
                        legend.text.align = NULL,
                        legend.title = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8, face = "bold", hjust = 0),
                        legend.title.align = NULL,
                        legend.position = "right",
                        legend.direction = NULL,
                        legend.box = NULL,
                        panel.background = theme_blank(),
                        panel.border = theme_blank(),
                        panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
                        panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(),
                        panel.margin = unit(0.25, "lines"),
                        strip.background = theme_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA),
                        strip.text.x = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8),
                        strip.text.y = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 0.8, angle = -90),
                        plot.background = theme_blank(),
                        plot.title = theme_text(family = base_family, size = base_size * 1.2),
                        plot.margin = unit(c(1, 1, 0.5, 0.5), "lines")),
                  class = "options")
     }

messages.subject: Re: theme_<journal_name> library
messages.body_plain:
There has been some discussion on this mailing list, but the outcome
is usually that very few people do share their themes. The examples on
the wiki are probably a start, but it would be nice to expand the
collection, share ideas to converge towards elegant and well-thought
designs, and perhaps use the feedback to fine-tune the choice of
default themes included in ggplot2 too:

- maybe some default themes could use minor tweaks. For instance I
find the strip background of theme_bw() too heavy; I almost always
change it to something lighter or even white. That's in fact the main
reason I wrote my version of theme_minimal()

- theme_minimal() or some version of it seems quite popular, as well
as theme_fullpage() (no margins). Maybe these two could be included in
the main package instead of seeing multiple versions being posted in
different places (and sometimes lacking proper updates)?

- there was some discussion on whether the modifyList() approach could
become the default definition of a new theme, all based on
theme_grey() maybe. I'm not sure where this idea was left in the end.
The basic design of themes is still a subject of debate every now and
then, I'm not sure a completely satisfying design has been agreed
upon.

Cheers,

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: cleaning up a plot
messages.body_plain:
> This works well.  Is there a way to remove the unused parameter labels by row in the grid?

Ugh, this starts to get ugly; pretty sure you need to use multiple
viewports for this kind of thing. I guess I'd do it something like
below, which should get you started, but you'll want to adjust the
grid.layout values and plot margins so things line up and look nice.
As far as I know, trial and error is the only way here.

Good luck-

Ben

d <- read.csv("ivmdz2.csv")

library(ggplot2)
library(grid)

# First, build the four panels
plots <- list(NULL)
theme_set(theme_bw())
for(i in unique(d$Drug)) {
	d1 <- droplevels(subset(d, Drug==i, drop=T))
	p <- ggplot(d1, aes(x=Parameter, y=Mean, ymin=Lo, ymax=Hi))
	p <- p  + geom_point(size=3, shape=5) + geom_errorbar() +
coord_flip() + geom_hline(aes(yintercept=0), lty=2) +
scale_y_continuous(limits=c(-1, 3))
	plots[[i]] <- p
}

#pdf("ivmdz2.pdf", width=4, height=6)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(2, 2)))
vplayout<-function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row=x, layout.pos.col=y)

# Now plot them in the four regions, adjusting margins and axis text
as necessary
print(plots[["DRUG 1"]] + opts(plot.margin=unit(c(1,0,0,0), "lines"),
axis.text.x=theme_blank(), axis.title.x=theme_blank()),
vp=vplayout(1,1))
print(plots[["DRUG 2"]] + opts(plot.margin=unit(c(1,1,0,0), "lines"),
axis.text.x=theme_blank(), axis.title.x=theme_blank(),
axis.title.y=theme_blank()), vp=vplayout(1,2))
print(plots[["DRUG 3"]] + opts(plot.margin=unit(c(0,0,0,0), "lines")),
vp=vplayout(2,1))
print(plots[["DRUG 4"]] + opts(plot.margin=unit(c(0,1,0,0), "lines"),
axis.title.y=theme_blank()), vp=vplayout(2,2))

#dev.off()

I was exploring the example ggplot2 time series heatmap example given
at http://margintale.blogspot.co.uk/2012/04/ggplot2-time-series-heatmaps.html
but whenever I re-create the plot the VIX.Close and the Week of the
Month are listed in 1e+01, 2e+01, etc... format.  How can I avoid this
format?  Code posted below:

###### Loading libraries
require(quantmod)
require(ggplot2)
require(reshape2)
require(plyr)
require(scales)
Sys.setlocale("LC_ALL","English_United States.1252")
options(scipen=10)

# Download some Data, e.g. the CBOE VIX
getSymbols("^VIX",src="yahoo")

# Make a dataframe
dat<-data.frame(date=index(VIX),VIX)

# We will facet by year ~ month, and each subgraph will
# show week-of-month versus weekday
# the year is simple
# the month too
# but turn months into ordered facors to control the appearance/
ordering in the presentation
# the day of week is again easily found
# again turn into factors to control appearance/abbreviation and
ordering
# I use the reverse function rev here to order the week top down in
the graph
# you can cut it out to reverse week order

dat$year<-as.numeric(as.POSIXlt(dat$date)$year+1900)
dat$month<-as.numeric(as.POSIXlt(dat$date)$mon+1)
dat$monthf<-factor(dat
$month,levels=as.character(1:12),labels=c("Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"),ordered=TRUE)
dat$weekday = as.POSIXlt(dat$date)$wday
dat$weekdayf<-factor(dat
$weekday,levels=rev(1:7),labels=rev(c("Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri","Sat","Sun")),ordered=TRUE)

# the monthweek part is a bit trickier
# first a factor which cuts the data into month chunks
# then find the "week of year" for each day
# and now for each monthblock we normalize the week to start at 1

dat$yearmonth<-as.yearmon(dat$date)
dat$yearmonthf<-factor(dat$yearmonth)
dat$week <- as.numeric(format(dat$date,"%W"))
dat<-ddply(dat,.(yearmonthf),transform,monthweek=1+week-min(week))

# Now for the plot
P <-ggplot(dat, aes(monthweek, weekdayf, fill = VIX.Close)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") + facet_grid(year~monthf) +
scale_fill_gradient(low="red", high="yellow") +
    opts(title = "Time-Series Calendar Heatmap") +  xlab("Week of
Month") + ylab("")
P

messages.subject: reshape2 melt date handling
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Has anyone encountered a problem using the melt function of reshape2 with date columns? I've melted my data.frame containing two columns of POSIXct dates but the resulting value column has been converted to a numeric rather than retained as a date. Am I using melt incorrectly or have I misunderstood the melting process? Here's a little example that'll reproduce it.

messages.subject: Re: reshape2 melt date handling
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, Apr 28, 2012 at 6:21 PM, Alastair <alastai...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi,
>
> Has anyone encountered a problem using the melt function of reshape2 with
> date columns? I've melted my data.frame containing two columns of POSIXct
> dates but the resulting value column has been converted to a numeric rather
> than retained as a date. Am I using melt incorrectly or have I misunderstood
> the melting process? Here's a little example that'll reproduce it.
>
> library(reshape2)
> x <- seq(from = as.POSIXlt("2010-01-01", tz = "GMT"), length.out = 20, by =
> "mins")
> y <- seq(from = as.POSIXlt("2010-01-01", tz = "GMT"), length.out = 20, by =
> "secs")
> df <- data.frame(id = 1:20, start = x, end = y)
> melt.df <- melt(df, measure.var = c("start", "end")
> class(melt.df$value) # this'll be number rather than POSIXct

Yes, the number of seconds since the origin 1970-01-01 00:00:00. Just
redefine value as a POSIXct object from that origin:

melt.df$value <- as.POSIXct(melt.df$value, origin = '1970-01-01 00:00:00')
str(melt.df)     # verify that it is indeed POSIXct

If you're wondering why value is returning an integer from melt()
rather than a POSIXct object,

> storage.mode(df$start)     # ditto for df$end
[1] "integer"

The POSIXct class stores date/time values as the number of seconds
since January 1, 1970 (at 00:00:00). (Spector 2008, 'Data Manipulation
in R', the last sentence on p. 60 that continues onto the following
page.) I think this is a feature of melt() rather than a bug, but you
could always make a feature request :)

OTOH, if you use the reshape() function in base R, it will return the
values as POSIXct:

dfrshp <- reshape(df, idvar = 'id', varying = c('start', 'end'),
                       v.names = 'value', direction = 'long')
str(dfrshp)

BTW, questions pertaining to plyr and reshape(2) are more appropriate
for the manipulator listserve; go to http://had.co.nz/reshape/ to
subscribe to that list.

Dennis

% as.factor(c("D","E","F"))))

+ coord_flip()
+ scale_fill_manual(name="Color", values=c("blue","red"),
labels=c("Near Colorless","Colorless"))

Not a huge issue, but I am generating a bunch of these
programmatically on a regular basis, and post-processing the legend is
not really an option.

Thanks,

messages.subject: Re: theme_<journal_name> library
messages.body_plain:
I too think the ggplot2-dev mailing list is a good place to discuss
these developments. There are some open questions, I think, regarding
the scope and design of themes in ggplot2 that might influence the
rest of the package. For instance:

- Should themes include the ability to set default scales? (e.g range
of line widths and sizes, default colour scales). Default layer
aesthetic settings? (e.g if your theme has a black background, it
would make sense that, say, geom_text layers use a white colour by
default to be visible.

- What is the best data structure for themes? On one end, it should
have a tree-like inheritance where children share defaut settings from
parents (axis tick marks have by default the same colour as axis
lines, for example). At the other end, it should also allow setting a
maximum level of details, still keeping a fairly concise yet explicit
syntax (nested nested lists quickly become painful to write/modify).

(There are a few previous discussions on this list and github.)

Best,

baptiste

messages.subject: The standard errors example
messages.body_plain:
Originally I sent this as an email (containing 2 questions) directly to Hadley who requested I send them to the ggplot help list as separate questions (this is question 1):

I am asked to do bar plots for people pretty often using count data (my field is literacy so counting is a fairly common augment to qualitative analysis).  I feel funny (as in slightly unethical) about just providing count data with no error bars but saw here http://had.co.nz/ggplot2/docs/geom_errorbar.html you use error bars on what appears to be count data (very first example; 2nd figure).  That inspired me to learn how to calculate standard errors on count data which some kind folks at talkstats.com <http://talkstats.com> told me I could do (doesn't necessarily make sense to do so) so using the Poisson distribution.  So I created a function to calculate SE for count data that also gives me confidence intervals (also I know people use +/- 1  SE for the error bars as well but that's pretty easy to calculate as you did in your example).  Here's that function in a .txt script from my drop box (
http://dl.dropbox.com/u/61803503/SEerror.txt ).

When I try it on your data set, given in the link to the ggplot2 site above, I get very different standard errors (
http://dl.dropbox.com/u/61803503/SEerror.txt ).  Can you tell me if you just randomly made up the standard errors on your data set for demonstration purposes or if they are authentic?  If they're authentic may I ask how you calculated them?

Thanks
Tyler Rinker

messages.subject: Inquiring about glyphs
messages.body_plain:
Originally I sent this as an email (containing 2 questions) directly to Hadley who requested I send them to the ggplot help list as separate questions (this is question 2):

I love ggplot2, particularly the faceting (facet_grid) which lattice can do but with much less flexibility and intuition.  I've been working on a for fun project using state school assessment data and mapping it using ggplot2 as faceted chorolopleths (
http://www.talkstats.com/showthread.php/23324-An-R-learning-project-(feel-free-to-learn-with-me)?p=82365&viewfull=1#post82365 ).   I came across a similar map that has pie graphs plotted on it, at the same time I checked out Wilkinson's "The Grammar of Graphics" as a certain package maker cites this book as inspiration.  I now know what I was seeing was what Wilkinson calls glyphs.  I asked about doing this type of plotting on a map on stackoverflow (
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/10368180/plotting-pie-graphs-on-map-in-ggplot ).   The folks there didn't have a means of plotting them using ggplot but did provide some info which indicates of your possible intention to add glyphs to ggplot2 at some point (the paper baptise links to).

Is this a possibility, intention etc. for the future?

Thanks,Tyler Rinker

> http://dl.dropbox.com/u/61803503/SEerror.txt ).

  It occurs to me to wonder offhand if calculating means and +/-1.96
standard errors on the square-root scale and then back-transforming
might give similar (or even exact??) answers as fitting a Poisson
model for a single category and finding (back-transformed) CI.  (The
guess is based on the fact that the Poisson family uses var=mean as a
variance function ...)
   For binomial models there are some fairly detailed developments of
exact small-sample confidence intervals (see e.g Agresti _Categorical
Data Analysis_ pp. 18-21); http://www.jstor.org/stable/2685469 .
epitools:::binom.exact() implements a variety of these recipes.

For Poisson, I would proceed based on the information here:
http://www.math.mcmaster.ca/peter/s743/poissonalpha.html
http://www.jstor.org/stable/10.2307/3314762
Googling "poisson confidence intervals" gives lots of good stuff ...

These are all for the case where the data are known to be
Poisson-distributed.  In fact, if you have multiple counts per
category then you don't have to assume var=mean, you can allow for
overdispersion ...
